answer:
HEADLINE HYPOTHESIS: The data do not support a statistically reliable conclusion that race moderates the SES → degree-completion relationship. The joint SES × race interaction is not significant (χ²=1.81, df=2, p=0.405), and this holds under Firth bias-correction (p=0.382) and is invariant to the choice of reference race. The overall SES effect is positive but only marginal (OR ≈ 1.19 per SD, p=0.063). Point estimates suggest — but do not establish — a steeper SES gradient for Black respondents (OR 1.62/SD, p=0.018) than for White (1.26/SD, p=0.020) or Hispanic (1.01/SD, p=0.96) respondents; the Black–White slope contrast (OR-of-OR 1.56, p=0.018) is a single nominally-significant contrast inside a non-significant 2-df joint test. With only 28 Black and 19 Hispanic completers, the analysis is underpowered to confirm or refute moderation, so this pattern is suggestive, not conclusive.

RESULTS (all models converged; ORs per 1-SD of SES, covariates: ABILITY_z, PERCENTILE_z, sex, centered family size):

1) Main model (ref=White):
   SES (White slope): OR 1.191 (0.991–1.431), p=0.063
   SES×Black:        OR 1.312 (0.881–1.955), p=0.181
   SES×Hispanic:     OR 1.011 (0.630–1.624), p=0.963
   JOINT WARD TEST (SES×Black, SES×Hispanic): χ²=1.810, df=2, p=0.4045
   Slope contrasts vs White: Black Δ=0.446 log-odds/SD (OR-of-OR 1.563, p=0.018); Hispanic Δ=0.186 (OR-of-OR 1.204, p=0.420)
   Race main effects: Black OR 1.551 (p=0.066), Hispanic OR 1.308 (p=0.30) — not significant.
   Covariates: ABILITY OR 2.329 (p<0.001), PERCENTILE OR 1.831 (p<0.001), Male OR 0.765 (p=0.06), family size OR 0.594/child (p<0.001).

2) VIF: max 2.73 (ABILITY), all < 3 — no multicollinearity concern (ABILITY–PERCENTILE r=0.70 manageable).

3) Alternative reference (ref=Black): joint Wald identical, χ²=1.810, p=0.4045 — interaction conclusion is reference-invariant.

4) Stratified fits (full covariates; all three converged, no fallback needed):
   White (n=5337, 189 events): SES OR 1.257 (1.037–1.524), p=0.020
   Black (n=2113, 28 events):  SES OR 1.624 (1.085–2.431), p=0.018
   Hispanic (n=1323, 19 events): SES OR 1.013 (0.622–1.649), p=0.959
   Note: in the Black stratum PERCENTILE (OR 2.54, p=0.0006) — not ABILITY (p=0.18) — carries the academic-performance effect.

5) Firth sensitivity (implemented by hand — no Firth in the installed statsmodels; penalty gradient verified against finite differences of ½log|I| to 1e-5):
   Main model: coefficients within 0.005 of MLE; joint interaction p=0.382 (vs 0.405 MLE).
   Black stratum: SES OR 1.621 (1.090–2.411), p=0.017 — unchanged.
   Hispanic stratum: SES OR 1.009 (0.625–1.630), p=0.970 — unchanged.

INTERPRETATION: The pre-specified test for moderation (joint SES×race interaction) is not significant, and every robustness variant (Firth, alternative reference, stratified fits) reproduces the same picture. The data therefore do not support the hypothesis that racial lines differentially shape the SES–degree-completion link at conventional significance levels. The Black vs White slope contrast is the only nominally significant piece (p≈0.018, stable under Firth), but it is one contrast within a 2-df test that fails overall, and the Hispanic slope is estimable only to within OR 0.62–1.65 — a range that includes both "no SES effect" and a large one. Power limitation: with 19 Hispanic and 28 Black completers, the study can reliably detect only very large differences in SES slopes; "no significant moderation" here is partly a statement about detectable effect size, not proof that the slopes are equal. Secondary caveat (from plan): adjusting for ABILITY (r=0.46 with SES) estimates a more direct SES effect, so the marginal main SES effect (p=0.063) should not be read as "SES does nothing."

payload.hypothesis: The data do not support a statistically reliable conclusion that race moderates the SES–degree-completion relationship: the joint SES×race interaction in a logistic model controlling for ABILITY composite, class percentile, sex, and family size is not significant (χ²=1.81, df=2, p=0.405; Firth-corrected p=0.382; reference-invariant). The overall SES effect is positive but marginal (OR≈1.19 per SD, p=0.063). Point estimates suggest a steeper SES gradient for Black respondents (OR 1.62/SD, p=0.018) than for White (1.26/SD, p=0.020) or Hispanic (1.01/SD, p=0.96) respondents, with the Black–White contrast nominally significant (OR-of-OR 1.56, p=0.018) but unstable against the failed joint test. Given only 28 Black and 19 Hispanic completers, the study is underpowered to confirm or refute moderation, so this pattern is suggestive rather than conclusive.
